title: Abundance and dispersed-knowledge lens
note: This is an analytical checklist, not a claim that every restriction is undesirable. Record the public purpose, distributional effects, externalities, and evidence alongside any cost to entry, supply, price discovery, or local experimentation.

rubric.incidence: Who receives the benefit and who bears the monetary, time, uncertainty, or exclusion cost?
rubric.evidence: What happened to quantities, prices, quality, informality, delay, concentration, and access after adoption or reform?

land.label: Land and housing
questions: Does zoning, land-use classification, or conversion permission prevent housing, commerce, or industry where demand exists?
Do floor-area ratios, height limits, setbacks, parking mandates, plot-size rules, or density caps restrict built supply?
How many permissions, agencies, hearings, and discretionary approvals are required, and how predictable are their time limits?
Are titles, cadastral maps, mutation, registration, and liens legible enough for strangers to transact without local political knowledge?
Do agricultural land ceilings or purchaser-eligibility rules fragment holdings or bar non-farmers, firms, or migrants from entry?
Do rent controls, eviction rules, circle rates, stamp duty, property tax, or vacant-land taxes suppress price discovery or create lock-in?
Do acquisition, environmental, heritage, forest, coastal, tribal-rights, or rehabilitation rules internalise real harms proportionately, or operate as an indefinite veto?
Who captures the rise in land value created by public infrastructure, and do development charges finance enough new infrastructure?
Can municipalities and neighbourhoods experiment with rule changes, or is every adjustment centralised at state level?

labour.label: Labour
questions: Which minimum wage, wage-board award, or compensation floor applies, and does it vary by skill, occupation, zone, age, or firm size?
Do dismissal, retrenchment, closure, standing-order, or contract-labour permissions change firms' willingness to hire formally?
Which payroll taxes and mandatory benefits raise the gap between what an employer pays and a worker receives?
Do occupational licences, educational credentials, domicile rules, or union-entry rules keep capable people from offering a service?
Are working-time, scheduling, night-work, and shop-opening rules safety protections, coordination devices, or barriers to flexible exchange?
Can benefits follow a worker across firms, states, informal work, and platforms, or do they bind the worker to one employer or registration?
Does enforcement protect vulnerable workers consistently, or mainly push small firms and workers into informality and official discretion?
What bargaining or information failure is the rule addressing, and is collective choice possible without excluding outsiders?

capital.label: Capital and enterprise
questions: Who may start, finance, own, or close an enterprise, and which licences, quotas, net-worth tests, or local no-objection certificates constrain entry?
Are interest rates, credit targets, priority-sector shares, collateral rules, or loan prices set administratively rather than discovered by lenders and borrowers?
Do foreign-investment caps, capital controls, localisation rules, or approval routes prevent capital and knowledge from reaching productive uses?
How quickly can failed firms, collateral, and labour be reorganised, sold, or released through insolvency and enforcement?
Do securities, company, audit, and disclosure rules scale with risk and firm size, or impose fixed costs that entrench incumbents?
Do subsidies, guarantees, public-bank direction, or tax preferences socialise downside risk while concentrating upside or political discretion?
Can new payment, insurance, energy, transport, and platform models enter through clear rules or a sandbox, or must they fit an incumbent category?
Are government contracts and concessions awarded through open, comparable bids with performance data and a credible path to replacement?

tax.label: Tax and administered prices
questions: Which taxes fall on transactions, construction, employment, investment, or moving assets rather than on less-distortive bases?
Do multiple rates, exemptions, cesses, and classification disputes obscure prices and reward lobbying or vertical integration?
Which prices are fixed, capped, supported, cross-subsidised, or compensated after the fact, and what shortages or surpluses follow?
Is the effective burden predictable before a citizen acts, including compliance time, blocked refunds, inspections, and litigation?
Does fiscal federalism let states and municipalities experiment while making the cost of local choices visible to local voters?

utilities.label: Utilities and infrastructure
questions: Is the network a natural monopoly, and if so are operations competitively tendered or benchmarked while the bottleneck remains regulated?
Who sets tariffs, connection charges, service standards, and cross-subsidies, and can users observe cost and reliability?
Can supply expand when demand rises, or do permits, fuel allocation, water rights, price caps, and weak cost recovery ration it indirectly?
If a private concessionaire operates the service, was it chosen through an open auction, what exactly was bid, and when can it be replaced?
Are universal-service and environmental goals funded transparently, or hidden in prices that deter new supply and maintenance?

rfctlarr-2013.note: Consent, social-impact and rehabilitation safeguards price displacement costs into projects, but can also lengthen or prevent land assembly. Compare delay and compensation outcomes, including state amendments.

registration-1908.note: Registration can make rights legible to strangers; high fees, incomplete title assurance, and slow mutation can instead freeze transactions.

stamp-1899.note: A transaction tax raises the cost of moving land to a higher-valued use and can encourage under-reporting; evaluate it with state rates and circle values.

pesa-1996.note: Local consent can incorporate knowledge and rights missed by a distant allocator; outcomes depend on whether deliberation is representative and time-bounded.

fra-2006.note: Recognising previously informal rights can enable stewardship and exchange while constraining projects that ignore those rights.

rera-2016.note: Disclosure and escrow can reduce information asymmetry and expand buyer trust, while fixed registration and compliance costs may burden small projects.

code-wages-2019.note: Compare gains for covered workers with hours, hiring, automation, enforcement, and informality, separately by local labour market.

code-ir-2020.note: Measure formal hiring, firm-size bunching, dispute duration, worker security, and closure or reorganisation time around relevant thresholds.

code-ss-2020.note: Portable benefits can improve mobility; contribution design and registration can also widen the formal-informal cost wedge.

code-osh-2020.note: Test whether risk-based, predictable safety enforcement improves welfare without making small formal workplaces unviable.

companies-2013.note: Disclosure enables impersonal investment, but fixed governance and filing costs should be compared across firm size and risk.

sebi-1992.note: Investor protection can deepen capital markets; examine whether approvals and intermediary rules unnecessarily exclude new products and small issuers.

fema-1999.note: Map automatic versus approval routes and test whether remaining controls target systemic risk proportionately or block information-bearing capital flows.

ibc-2016.note: Time-bound exit can release assets for new uses; measure actual duration, recovery, liquidation, and the effect of tribunal capacity.

sarfaesi-2002.note: Faster collateral enforcement may expand credit supply, balanced against due process and the market quality of asset sales.

gst-2017.note: A common market reduces border and cascading costs, while rate complexity, working-capital blockage, and compliance costs can disadvantage small firms.

it-2025.note: Evaluate marginal effective rates, neutrality across legal forms and assets, predictability, compliance time, and investment response—not only headline rates.
